title: How to work with Policies in ASP.NET Core Identity
description: Create and apply authorization policies for role and claim-based access control.

data.text: An **authorization policy** is a named collection of requirements a user must satisfy to access a resource. Policies combine one or more role requirements, claim requirements, or custom requirements into a single reusable rule.

terms.definition: A named set of requirements registered in Program.cs. Applied with [Authorize(Policy = "PolicyName")].
Marker interface for a custom requirement. Implement it to define your own authorization logic.
Evaluates a specific IAuthorizationRequirement. Calls context.Succeed() or context.Fail().
Extension method on AuthorizationOptions that registers a new named policy.
Injected service that lets you evaluate policies imperatively from within controller code.

data.definition:
flowchart TD
    A[Request hits [Authorize Policy=X]] --> B[Load policy requirements]
    B --> C{RequireRole met?}
    C -->|No| Z[Access Denied]
    C -->|Yes| D{RequireClaim met?}
    D -->|No| Z
    D -->|Yes| E{Custom requirements?}
    E -->|No| Y[Access Granted]
    E -->|Yes| F[Run AuthorizationHandler]
    F -->|Succeed| Y
    F -->|Fail| Z

data.title: Exercise: Build a Department-Based Policy
data.description: Create a policy that only allows users with a Department claim equal to HR to access an action.
steps: In Program.cs, add a policy called "HROnly" that requires claim type Department with value HR.
Create a ClaimsController action that lets HR users add the Department claim to themselves.
Log in as a user without the claim — confirm Access Denied.
Add the Department=HR claim, re-login, and access the Reports action.
data.expectedOutcome: The Reports action is only accessible to users with Department=HR claim. Adding the claim unlocks access after re-login.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Policies combine role, claim, and custom requirements into reusable rules.
AddPolicy registers a named policy; [Authorize(Policy = "...")] applies it.
Custom requirements need an IAuthorizationRequirement class and an AuthorizationHandler.
IAuthorizationService enables imperative policy checks inside action code.
data.takeaway: Policies are the most flexible way to control access in Identity. Next, enforce who can do what with role-based authorization.
